claim: Real-world scenes have inherent correlations between visual and semantic features.
source: Inherent correlations between visual and semantic features in real-world scenes make it difficult to determine how different scene properties contribute to neural representations.
evidence: This is stated as a premise in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Behavioral assessments of scene similarity reflected unique contributions from a functional feature model indicating potential actions in scenes.
source: Behavioral assessments of scene similarity reflected unique contributions from a functional feature model indicating potential actions in scenes as well as high-level visual features from a deep neural network (DNN).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Behavioral assessments of scene similarity reflected unique contributions from high-level visual features from a deep neural network (DNN).
source: Behavioral assessments of scene similarity reflected unique contributions from a functional feature model indicating potential actions in scenes as well as high-level visual features from a deep neural network (DNN).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Similarity of cortical responses in scene-selective areas was uniquely explained by mid- and high-level DNN features only.
source: In contrast, similarity of cortical responses in scene-selective areas was uniquely explained by mid- and high-level DNN features only, while an object label model did not contribute uniquely to either domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by fMRI data shown in Figures 3 and 8.

claim: An object label model did not contribute uniquely to behavioral or brain representations of scenes.
source: In contrast, similarity of cortical responses in scene-selective areas was uniquely explained by mid- and high-level DNN features only, while an object label model did not contribute uniquely to either domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: There is a striking dissociation between functional and DNN features in their contribution to behavioral and brain representations of scenes.
source: The striking dissociation between functional and DNN features in their contribution to behavioral and brain representations of scenes indicates that scene-selective cortex represents only a subset of behaviorally relevant scene information.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by the combined results from Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Scene-selective cortex represents only a subset of behaviorally relevant scene information.
source: The striking dissociation between functional and DNN features in their contribution to behavioral and brain representations of scenes indicates that scene-selective cortex represents only a subset of behaviorally relevant scene information.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion inferred from the dissociation between behavioral and brain data.

claim: The human brain contains three scene-selective regions: the Parahippocampal Place Area (PPA), Occipital Place Area (OPA), and Medial Place Area (MPA).
source: In the human brain, the perception of complex scenes is characterized by the activation of three scene-selective regions, the Parahippocampal Place Area (PPA; Aguirre et al., 1998; Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998), Occipital Place Area (OPA; Hasson et al., 2002; Dilks et al., 2013), and Medial Place Area (MPA; Silson et al., 2016), also referred to as the Retrosplenial Complex (Bar and Aminoff, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: MPA is also referred to as the Retrosplenial Complex.
source: In the human brain, the perception of complex scenes is characterized by the activation of three scene-selective regions, the Parahippocampal Place Area (PPA; Aguirre et al., 1998; Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998), Occipital Place Area (OPA; Hasson et al., 2002; Dilks et al., 2013), and Medial Place Area (MPA; Silson et al., 2016), also referred to as the Retrosplenial Complex (Bar and Aminoff, 2003).
evidence: This is stated explicitly with citation support.

claim: There are inherent correlations between semantic category, layout and spatial frequency in scenes.
source: For example, forests are characterized by the presence of spatial boundaries and numerous vertical edges, whereas beaches are typically open with a prominent horizon, resulting in correlations between semantic category, layout and spatial frequency (Oliva and Torralba, 2001; Torralba and Oliva, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as an example with citation support.

claim: Forests are characterized by the presence of spatial boundaries and numerous vertical edges.
source: For example, forests are characterized by the presence of spatial boundaries and numerous vertical edges, whereas beaches are typically open with a prominent horizon, resulting in correlations between semantic category, layout and spatial frequency (Oliva and Torralba, 2001; Torralba and Oliva, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as an example of inherent feature correlations.

claim: Beaches are typically open with a prominent horizon.
source: For example, forests are characterized by the presence of spatial boundaries and numerous vertical edges, whereas beaches are typically open with a prominent horizon, resulting in correlations between semantic category, layout and spatial frequency (Oliva and Torralba, 2001; Torralba and Oliva, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as an example of inherent feature correlations.

claim: Due to inherent feature correlations, spatial frequency, subjective distance and semantic properties explained the same variance in fMRI responses to real-world scenes.
source: Indeed, an explicit test of spatial frequency, subjective distance and semantic properties found that due to inherent feature correlations, all three properties explained the same variance in fMRI responses to real-world scenes (Lescroart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: The three models that contributed most to human scene categorization in Greene et al. (2016) were a functional model, a DNN model, and an object model.
source: The three models that contributed most to human scene categorization were (1) a model based on human-assigned labels of actions that can be carried out in the scene ('functional model'), (2) a deep convolutional neural network ('DNN model') that was trained to map visual features natural images to a set of a 1000 image classes from the ImageNet database (Deng et al., 2009), and (3) human-assigned labels for all the objects in the scene ('object model').
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Greene et al. (2016) with citation.

claim: The DNN model was trained to map visual features of natural images to a set of 1000 image classes from the ImageNet database.
source: The three models that contributed most to human scene categorization were (1) a model based on human-assigned labels of actions that can be carried out in the scene ('functional model'), (2) a deep convolutional neural network ('DNN model') that was trained to map visual features natural images to a set of a 1000 image classes from the ImageNet database (Deng et al., 2009), and (3) human-assigned labels for all the objects in the scene ('object model').
evidence: This describes the DNN model used in the study.

claim: A stimulus selection procedure was implemented that reduced inherent correlations between the three models of interest a priori.
source: To address the second challenge, we implemented a stimulus selection procedure that reduced inherent correlations between the three models of interest a priori.
evidence: This is a methodological approach described in the manuscript.

claim: Thirty scene categories were selected in which the three RDMs were minimally correlated (Pearson's r: 0.23–0.26).
source: Thus, a final selection of 30 scene categories was selected in which the three RDMs were minimally correlated (Pearson's r: 0.23–0.26; Figure 1B–C; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological result describing the stimulus selection.

claim: All three feature models were significantly correlated with scene categorization behavior.
source: Replicating Greene et al. (2016), this analysis indicated that all three feature models were significantly correlated with scene categorization behavior, with the function model having the highest correlation on average (Figure 2C; objects: mean r = 0.16; DNN features: mean r = 0.26; functions: mean r = 0.29, Wilcoxon one-sided signed-rank test, all W(20) > 210, all z > 3.9, all p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the behavioral experiment with statistical support.

claim: The function model had the highest correlation with scene categorization behavior on average (mean r = 0.29).
source: Replicating Greene et al. (2016), this analysis indicated that all three feature models were significantly correlated with scene categorization behavior, with the function model having the highest correlation on average (Figure 2C; objects: mean r = 0.16; DNN features: mean r = 0.26; functions: mean r = 0.29, Wilcoxon one-sided signed-rank test, all W(20) > 210, all z > 3.9, all p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the behavioral experiment with statistical support.

claim: The correlation with functions was higher than with objects (W(20) = 199, z = 3.5, p=0.0004).
source: The correlation with functions was higher than with objects (Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank test, W(20) = 199, z = 3.5, p=0.0004), but not than with DNN features (W(20) = 134, z = 1.1, p=0.28), which also correlated higher than objects (W(20) = 194, z = 3.3, p=0.0009).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the behavioral data.

claim: The correlation with functions was not significantly higher than with DNN features (W(20) = 134, z = 1.1, p=0.28).
source: The correlation with functions was higher than with objects (Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank test, W(20) = 199, z = 3.5, p=0.0004), but not than with DNN features (W(20) = 134, z = 1.1, p=0.28), which also correlated higher than objects (W(20) = 194, z = 3.3, p=0.0009).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the behavioral data.

claim: DNN features correlated higher than objects with scene categorization behavior (W(20) = 194, z = 3.3, p=0.0009).
source: The correlation with functions was higher than with objects (Wilcoxon two-sided signed-rank test, W(20) = 199, z = 3.5, p=0.0004), but not than with DNN features (W(20) = 134, z = 1.1, p=0.28), which also correlated higher than objects (W(20) = 194, z = 3.3, p=0.0009).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the behavioral data.

claim: Functions outperformed both the DNN and object models for the majority of participants (n = 12 for functions, n = 7 for DNN features, n = 1 for objects).
source: However, comparison at the level of individual participants indicated that functions outperformed both the DNN and object models for the majority of participants (highest correlation with functions: n = 12; with DNN features: n = 7; with objects: n = 1; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from individual participant analysis.

claim: Each model independently contributed to the behavioral data as shown by significant partial correlations.
source: The results indicated that each model independently contributed to the behavioral data: significant partial correlations were obtained for the object (W(20) = 173, z = 2.5, p=0.006), DNN features (W(20) = 209, z = 3.9, p<0.0001) and function models (W(20) = 209, z = 3.9, p<0.0001), with the function model having the largest partial correlation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from partial correlation analysis with statistical support.

claim: A full model including all three models explained 50.3% of the variance in the average multi-arrangement behavior.
source: A full model in which all three models were included explained 50.3% of the variance in the average multi-arrangement behavior (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a result from variance partitioning analysis.

claim: The largest portion of variance in multi-arrangement behavior could be uniquely attributed to the function model (unique r2 = 37.6%).
source: Highlighting the importance of functional features for scene categorization, the largest portion of this variance could be uniquely attributed to the function model (unique r2 = 37.6%), more than the unique variance explained by the DNN features (unique r2 = 29.0%) or the objects (unique r2 = 1.4%).
evidence: This is a result from variance partitioning analysis.

claim: DNN features explained unique variance of 29.0% in multi-arrangement behavior.
source: Highlighting the importance of functional features for scene categorization, the largest portion of this variance could be uniquely attributed to the function model (unique r2 = 37.6%), more than the unique variance explained by the DNN features (unique r2 = 29.0%) or the objects (unique r2 = 1.4%).
evidence: This is a result from variance partitioning analysis.

claim: Objects explained unique variance of 1.4% in multi-arrangement behavior.
source: Highlighting the importance of functional features for scene categorization, the largest portion of this variance could be uniquely attributed to the function model (unique r2 = 37.6%), more than the unique variance explained by the DNN features (unique r2 = 29.0%) or the objects (unique r2 = 1.4%).
evidence: This is a result from variance partitioning analysis.

claim: The scene similarity reflected in the multi-arrangement behavior was highly generalizable, with an RDM correlation of r = 0.73 across two different sets of scene exemplars.
source: Importantly, a reproducibility test indicated that the scene similarity reflected in the multi-arrangement behavior was highly generalizable, resulting in an RDM correlation of r = 0.73 (95% confidence interval = [0.73–0.88], p=0.0001) across two different sets of scene exemplars that were evenly distributed across participants (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a result from a reproducibility test.

claim: All three feature models correlated with the fMRI response patterns in PPA.
source: Similar to the behavioral findings, all three feature models correlated with the fMRI response patterns in PPA (objects: W(20) = 181, z = 2.8, p=0.002; DNN: W(20) = 206, z = 3.8, p<0.0001; functions: W(20) = 154, z = 1.8, p=0.035, see Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI analysis with statistical support.

claim: PPA correlated more strongly with the DNN feature model than the object and function models.
source: However, PPA correlated more strongly with the DNN feature model than the object (W(20) = 195, z = 2.5, p=0.012) and function (W(20) = 198, z = 3.5, p<0.0005) models, which did not differ from one another (W(20) = 145, z = 1.5, p=0.14).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI analysis with statistical support.

claim: In OPA, only the DNN model correlated with the fMRI response patterns (W(20) = 165, z = 2.2, p=0.013).
source: In OPA, only the DNN model correlated with the fMRI response patterns (W(20) = 165, z = 2,2, p=0.013), and this correlation was again stronger than for the object model (W(20) = 172, z = 2.5, p=0.012), but not the function model (W(20) = 134, z = 1.1, p=0.28).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI analysis with statistical support.

claim: In MPA, no correlations with the three models were significant.
source: In MPA, no correlations were significant (all W(14) < 76, all z < 1.4, all p>0.07).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI analysis with statistical support.

claim: Only the DNN model yielded a significant partial correlation in PPA (W(20) = 203, z = 3.6, p<0.0001) and OPA (W(20) = 171, z = 2.5, p=0.007).
source: When the three models were considered in combination, only the DNN model yielded a significant partial correlation (PPA: W(20) = 203, z = 3.6, p<0.0001, OPA: W(20) = 171, z = 2.5, p=0.007, Figure 3C), further showing that DNN features best capture responses in scene-selective cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from partial correlation analysis with statistical support.

claim: In PPA, DNN features contributed 71.1% of the variance explained by all models combined.
source: Variance partitioning of the fMRI RDMs (Figure 3D) indicated that the DNN model also contributed the largest portion of unique variance: in PPA and OPA, DNN features contributed 71.1% and 68.9%, respectively, of the variance explained by all models combined, more than the unique variance explained by the object (PPA: 5.3%; OPA, 2.3%) and function (PPA: 0.3%; OPA: 2.6%) models.
evidence: This is a result from variance partitioning analysis.

claim: In OPA, DNN features contributed 68.9% of the variance explained by all models combined.
source: Variance partitioning of the fMRI RDMs (Figure 3D) indicated that the DNN model also contributed the largest portion of unique variance: in PPA and OPA, DNN features contributed 71.1% and 68.9%, respectively, of the variance explained by all models combined, more than the unique variance explained by the object (PPA: 5.3%; OPA, 2.3%) and function (PPA: 0.3%; OPA: 2.6%) models.
evidence: This is a result from variance partitioning analysis.

claim: RDMs generalized across participants and stimulus sets for PPA (r = 0.26, p=0.009) and OPA (r = 0.23, p=0.0148), but not in MPA (r = 0.06, p=0.29).
source: A reproducibility test indicated that RDMs generalized across participants and stimulus sets for PPA (r = 0.26 [0.03–0.54], p=0.009) and OPA (r = 0.23 [0.04–0.51], p=0.0148), but not in MPA (r = 0.06 [−0.16–0.26], p=0.29), suggesting that the multi-voxel patterns measured in MPA were less stable (this is also reflected in the low noise ceiling in MPA in Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is a result from a reproducibility test.

claim: Deep network features best explained the coding of scene information in PPA and OPA, more so than object or functional information.
source: Taken together, the fMRI results indicate that of the three models considered, deep network features (derived using a pre-trained convolutional network) best explained the coding of scene information in PPA and OPA, more so than object or functional information derived from semantic labels that were explicitly generated by human observers.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the fMRI results.

claim: In PPA, all three measures of behavioral categorization correlated with fMRI responses.
source: In PPA, all three measures of behavioral categorization correlated with fMRI responses (signed-rank test, online categorization behavior: W(20) = 168, z = 2.3, p=0.010; average multi-arrangement behavior: W(20) = 195, z = 3.3, p=0.0004; own arrangement behavior: W(20) = 159, z = 2.0, p=0.023).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis with statistical support.

claim: In OPA, significant correlations were found for both of the average behavioral measures but not for the participant's own multi-arrangement behavior.
source: In OPA, significant correlations were found for both of the average behavioral measures (online categorization behavior: W(20) = 181, z = 2.8, p=0.002; average multi-arrangement behavior: W(20) = 158, z = 1.96, p=0.025), but not for the participant's own multi-arrangement behavior (W(20) = 106, z = 0.02, p=0.49), possibly due to higher noise in the individual data.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis with statistical support.

claim: In MPA, participant's own behavior was significantly related to the observed fMRI responses (W(14) = 89, z = 2.26, p=0.011), but the average behavioral measures were not.
source: Interestingly, however, MPA showed the opposite pattern: participant's own behavior was significantly related to the observed fMRI responses (W(14) = 89, z = 2.26, p=0.011), but the average behavioral measures were not (online behavior: W(14) = 47, z = 0.4, p=0.65; average behavior: W(14) = 74, z = 1.3, p=0.09).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis with statistical support.

claim: In OPA and PPA, most of the behavioral variance in the fMRI response patterns was shared with the DNN model.
source: Consistent with this second hypothesis, the variance partitioning results indicated that in OPA and PPA, most of the behavioral variance in the fMRI response patterns was shared with the DNN model (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from variance partitioning analysis.

claim: In PPA, the behavioral RDMs on average shared 25.7% variance with the DNN model, while a negligible portion was shared with the function model (less than 1%).
source: In PPA, the behavioral RDMs on average shared 25.7% variance with the DNN model, while a negligible portion was shared with the function model (less than 1%); indeed, nearly all variance shared between the function model and the behavior was also shared with the DNN model (10.1%).
evidence: This is a result from variance partitioning analysis.

claim: In OPA, behavior shared 38.9% of the fMRI variance with the DNN model.
source: In OPA, a similar trend was observed, with behavior sharing 38.9% of the fMRI variance with the DNN model.
evidence: This is a result from variance partitioning analysis.

claim: fMRI response patterns in PPA and OPA reflect information that contributes to scene similarity judgments, and this information aligns best with the DNN feature model.
source: In sum, while fMRI response patterns in PPA and OPA reflect information that contributes to scene similarity judgments, this information aligns best with the DNN feature model; it does not reflect the unique contribution of functions to scene categorization behavior.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on variance partitioning results.

claim: Experiment 2 yielded similar results as Experiment 1 despite the task difference.
source: Despite this task difference, Experiment 2 yielded similar results as Experiment 1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the two experiments.

claim: Overall model correlations were considerably higher in Experiment 2 than in Experiment 1.
source: Reflecting participant's enhanced engagement with the scenes when performing the covert naming task, overall model correlations were considerably higher than in Experiment 1, and now yielded significant correlations with the function model in both OPA and MPA (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the two experiments.

claim: In all three ROIs in Experiment 2, the DNN model correlations were significantly stronger than the function and object model correlations.
source: Importantly, in all three ROIs, the DNN model correlations were again significantly stronger than the function and object model correlations, which again contributed very little unique variance (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 2.

claim: In PPA and OPA, the naming task resulted in increased correlations for the DNN model only (PPA: p=0.0048; OPA p=0.0056).
source: Direct comparison of RDM correlations across the two Experiments indicated that in PPA and OPA, the naming task resulted in increased correlations for the DNN model only (two-sided Wilcoxon ranksum test, PPA: p=0.0048; OPA p=0.0056), without any difference in correlations for the other models (all p>0.52).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the two experiments with statistical support.

claim: The strong contribution of DNN features to fMRI responses in scene-selective cortex is not likely the result of limited engagement of participants with the scenes when viewed in the scanner.
source: In sum, the results of Experiment 2 indicate that the strong contribution of DNN features to fMRI responses in scene-selective cortex is not likely the result of limited engagement of participants with the scenes when viewed in the scanner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Enhanced attention to the scenes under an explicit naming instruction resulted in even stronger representation of the DNN features, without a clear increase in contributions of the function or object models.
source: If anything, enhanced attention to the scenes under an explicit naming instruction resulted in even stronger representation of the DNN features, without a clear increase in contributions of the function or object models.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: For the DNN feature model, significant searchlight clusters were found in PPA and OPA, but not MPA.
source: The results of these searchlight analyses were entirely consistent with the ROI analyses: for the DNN feature model, significant searchlight clusters were found in PPA and OPA (Figure 6A), but not MPA, whereas no significant clusters were found for the function model in any of the scene-selective ROIs.
evidence: This is a finding from searchlight analysis.

claim: No significant clusters were found for the function model in any of the scene-selective ROIs.
source: The results of these searchlight analyses were entirely consistent with the ROI analyses: for the DNN feature model, significant searchlight clusters were found in PPA and OPA (Figure 6A), but not MPA, whereas no significant clusters were found for the function model in any of the scene-selective ROIs.
evidence: This is a finding from searchlight analysis.

claim: Two clusters were identified for the function model outside of scene-selective cortex: a bilateral cluster on the ventral surface and a unilateral cluster on the left lateral surface.
source: However, two clusters were identified for the function model outside of scene-selective cortex (Figure 6B): 1) a bilateral cluster on the ventral surface, lateral to PPA, overlapping with the fusiform and temporal lateral gyri, and 2) a unilateral cluster on the left lateral surface, located adjacent to, but more ventral than, OPA, overlapping the posterior middle and inferior temporal gyrus.
evidence: This is a finding from searchlight analysis.

claim: A significant searchlight correlation was found between the behavioral measurements and response patterns in PPA and OPA.
source: Consistent with the results reported in Figure 4, we found a significant searchlight correlation between the behavioral measurements and response patterns in PPA and OPA (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from searchlight analysis.

claim: Behavioral categorization did not correlate with any regions outside PPA and OPA, including the clusters that correlated with the function model.
source: Surprisingly, however, behavioral categorization did not correlate with any regions outside these ROIs, including the clusters that correlated with the function model.
evidence: This is a finding from searchlight analysis.

claim: Most of the scene categories that were strongly separated in the function model searchlight clusters contained scene exemplars depicting humans that performed actions.
source: Most of the scene categories that were strongly separated all contained scene exemplars depicting humans that performed actions (see Figure 7C), although it is worth noting that scene exemplars in the fourth most distinct category, 'volcano', did not contain any humans but may be characterized by implied motion.
evidence: This is an observation from post-hoc analysis of the searchlight results.

claim: The searchlight correlation with the functional feature model may be due to the presence of human-, body- and/or motion selective voxels in these searchlight clusters.
source: These post-hoc observations suggest that (parts of) the searchlight correlation with the functional feature model may be due to the presence of human-, body- and/or motion selective voxels in these searchlight clusters.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the searchlight results.

claim: The strongest contributions of the DNN model were found in scene-selective cortex.
source: In sum, the searchlight analyses indicate that the strongest contributions of the DNN model were found in scene-selective cortex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the searchlight analyses.

claim: Regions outside of scene-selective cortex that correlated with aspects of the function model did not appear to contribute to the scene categorization behavior.
source: While some aspects of the function model may be reflected in regions outside of scene-selective cortex, these regions did not appear to contribute to the scene categorization behavior, and may reflect selectivity for only a subset of scene categories that clustered together in the function model.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the searchlight analyses.

claim: Both object-trained and scene-trained DNNs extracted similar features, evidenced by strong between-model correlations overall (all layers r > 0.6).
source: Direct comparisons of the layer-by-layer RDMs of these two DNNs (Figure 8A) indicated that both models extracted similar features, evidenced by strong between-model correlations overall (all layers r > 0.6).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing two DNNs.

claim: The similarity between object-trained and scene-trained DNNs decreased with higher layers.
source: However, the similarity between models decreased with higher layers, suggesting that features in higher DNN layers become tailored to the task they are trained on.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing two DNNs.

claim: Features in higher DNN layers become tailored to the task they are trained on.
source: However, the similarity between models decreased with higher layers, suggesting that features in higher DNN layers become tailored to the task they are trained on.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of two DNNs.

claim: The object-trained and the scene-trained DNN correlated similarly with PPA and OPA.
source: Layer-by-layer correlations of the object-trained (Figure 8C) and the scene-trained DNN (Figure 8D) with fMRI responses in PPA, OPA and MPA however did not indicate a strong difference in DNN performance as a result of training.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing DNN layers with fMRI data.

claim: In PPA, both the object-trained and place-trained DNN showed increased correlation with higher DNN layers.
source: In PPA, both the object-trained and place-trained DNN showed increased correlation with higher DNN layers, consistent with previous work showing a hierarchical mapping of DNN layers to low vs. high-level visual cortex (Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015; Cichy et al., 2016; Wen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from layer-by-layer analysis with citation support.

claim: In OPA, there was no evidence for increased performance with higher layers for the object-trained DNN.
source: In OPA, we observed no evidence for increased performance with higher layers for the object-trained DNN; none of the pairwise tests survived multiple comparisons correction.
evidence: This is a finding from layer-by-layer analysis.

claim: For the scene-trained DNN, the OPA correlation significantly decreased rather than increased with higher layers, showing a peak correlation with layer 3.
source: In fact, for the scene-trained DNN, the OPA correlation significantly decreased rather than increased with higher layers, showing a peak correlation with layer 3.
evidence: This is a finding from layer-by-layer analysis.

claim: Despite a divergence in representation in high-level layers for differently-trained DNNs, their performance in predicting brain responses in scene-selective cortex is quite similar.
source: These results indicate that despite a divergence in representation in high-level layers for differently-trained DNNs, their performance in predicting brain responses in scene-selective cortex is quite similar.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the layer-by-layer analysis.

claim: fMRI responses in scene-selective ROIs may reflect a contribution of visual DNN features of intermediate complexity rather than, or in addition to, the fc7 layer.
source: Therefore, these results suggest that fMRI responses in scene-selective ROIs may reflect a contribution of visual DNN features of intermediate complexity rather than, or in addition to, the fc7 layer that was selected a priori.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the layer-by-layer analysis.

claim: Behavioral scene categorization was best explained by a combination of the function model and DNN features.
source: Second, we found that brain responses to visual scenes in scene-selective regions were best explained by a DNN feature model, with no discernible unique contribution of functions. Thus, although parts of variance in the multi-arrangement behavior were captured by the DNN feature model - and this part of the behavior was reflected in the scene-selective cortex - there are clearly aspects of scene categorization behavior that were not reflected in the activity of these regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: There are aspects of scene categorization behavior that were not reflected in the activity of scene-selective regions.
source: Thus, although parts of variance in the multi-arrangement behavior were captured by the DNN feature model - and this part of the behavior was reflected in the scene-selective cortex - there are clearly aspects of scene categorization behavior that were not reflected in the activity of these regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the dissociation between behavioral and brain data.

claim: The searchlight clusters that correlated with the function model potentially overlap with known face- and body-selective regions such as FFA, FBA, and EBA.
source: Visual inspection of these maps suggests that these clusters potentially overlap with known face- and body-selective regions such as the Fusiform Face (FFA; Kanwisher et al., 1997) and Fusiform Body (FBA; Peelen and Downing, 2007) areas on ventral surface, as well as the Extrastriate Body Area (EBA; Downing et al., 2001) on the lateral surface.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on visual inspection of searchlight maps.

claim: The lateral cluster that correlated with the function model could possibly include motion-selective and tool-selective regions.
source: This lateral cluster could possibly include motion-selective (Zeki et al., 1991; Tootell et al., 1995) and tool-selective (Martin et al., 1996) regions as well.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation support.

claim: Lateral occipital-temporal cortex is thought to support action observation by containing representations which capture perceptual, semantic and motor knowledge of how actions change the state of the world.
source: Lateral occipital-temporal cortex in particular is thought to support action observation by containing 'representations which capture perceptual, semantic and motor knowledge of how actions change the state of the world' (Lingnau and Downing, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Scene functions only become relevant for scene categorization when participants are engaged in a contrastive task.
source: Therefore, one possibility is that scene functions only become relevant for scene categorization when participants are engaged in a contrastive task, that is explicitly comparing two scene exemplars side-by-side (as in Greene et al., 2016) or within the context of the entire stimulus set being present on the screen (as in our multi-arrangement paradigm).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the dissociation between behavioral and brain data.

claim: Not all the information that contributes to scene categorization is reflected in scene-selective cortex activity 'by default'.
source: Overall, our findings suggest that not all the information that contributes to scene categorization is reflected in scene-selective cortex activity 'by default', and that explicit task requirements may be necessary in order for this information to emerge in the neural activation patterns in these regions of cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the overall findings.

claim: Explicit task requirements may be necessary in order for functional information to emerge in the neural activation patterns in scene-selective regions of cortex.
source: Overall, our findings suggest that not all the information that contributes to scene categorization is reflected in scene-selective cortex activity 'by default', and that explicit task requirements may be necessary in order for this information to emerge in the neural activation patterns in these regions of cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings.

claim: There are potentially separate scene-selective networks for memory versus perception.
source: Furthermore, given reports of potentially separate scene-selective networks for memory versus perception (Baldassano et al., 2016; Silson et al., 2016), it is likely that differences in mnemonic demands between tasks may have an important influence on scene-selective cortex activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Memory-based navigation or place recognition tasks have been shown to more strongly engage the medial parietal cortex and MPA.
source: Indeed, memory-based navigation or place recognition tasks (Epstein et al., 2007; Marchette et al., 2014) have been shown to more strongly engage the medial parietal cortex and MPA.
evidence: This is established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The observed correlation with DNN features supports a primary role for PPA and OPA in bottom-up visual scene analysis.
source: In contrast, our observed correlation with DNN features seems to support a primary role for PPA and OPA in bottom-up visual scene analysis, and fits well with the growing literature showing correspondences between extrastriate cortex activity and DNN features (Cadieu et al., 2014; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015; Cichy et al., 2016; Horikawa and Kamitani, 2017; Wen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the findings with citation support.

claim: DNN correlations with scene-selective cortex were not exclusive to higher DNN layers, but already emerged at earlier layers.
source: Our analyses further showed that DNN correlations with scene-selective cortex were not exclusive to higher DNN layers, but already emerged at earlier layers, suggesting that the neural representation in PPA/OPA may be driven more by visual features than semantic information (Watson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the layer-by-layer analysis.

claim: The neural representation in PPA/OPA may be driven more by visual features than semantic information.
source: Our analyses further showed that DNN correlations with scene-selective cortex were not exclusive to higher DNN layers, but already emerged at earlier layers, suggesting that the neural representation in PPA/OPA may be driven more by visual features than semantic information (Watson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the layer-by-layer analysis with citation support.

claim: When participants perform scene categorization, they incorporate information that is not reflected in either the DNNs or in PPA and OPA.
source: However, our current results suggest that when participants perform scene categorization, either explicitly (Greene et al., 2016) or within a multi-arrangement paradigm (Kriegeskorte and Mur, 2012), they incorporate information that is not reflected in either the DNNs or in PPA and OPA.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the overall findings.

claim: There is a significant gap between the information that is captured in both scene–selective cortex and a set of commonly used off-the-shelf DNNs, relative to the information that drives human understanding of visual environments.
source: Our results thus highlight a significant gap between the information that is captured in both scene–selective cortex and a set of commonly used off-the-shelf DNNs, relative to the information that drives human understanding of visual environments.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the overall findings.

claim: Visual environments are highly multidimensional, and scene understanding encompasses many behavioral goals, including not just visual object or scene recognition, but also navigation and action planning.
source: Visual environments are highly multidimensional, and scene understanding encompasses many behavioral goals, including not just visual object or scene recognition, but also navigation and action planning (Malcolm et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge with citation support.

claim: It is probably not appropriate to think about the neural representations relevant to all different behavioral goals as being contained within one single brain region or a single neural network model.
source: While visual or DNN features likely feed into multiple of these goals - for example, by signaling navigable paths in the environment (Bonner and Epstein, 2017), or landmark suitability (Troiani et al., 2014) - it is probably not appropriate to think about the neural representations relevant to all these different behavioral goals as being contained within one single brain region or a single neural network model.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the findings with citation support.

claim: Unraveling the neural coding of scene information will require careful manipulations of both multiple tasks and multiple scene feature models.
source: Ultimately, unraveling the neural coding of scene information will require careful manipulations of both multiple tasks and multiple scene feature models, as well as a potential expansion of our focus on a broader set of regions than those characterized by the presence of scene-selectivity.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the findings.

claim: Out of three behaviorally relevant feature models, only the DNN model provided a robust correlation with activity in scene-selective cortex.
source: We successfully disentangled the type of information represented in scene-selective cortex: out of three behaviorally relevant feature models, only one provided a robust correlation with activity in scene-selective cortex. This model was derived from deep neural network features from a widely used computer vision algorithm for object and scene recognition.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The DNN model was not sufficient to explain scene categorization behavior, which was characterized by an additional strong contribution of functional information.
source: Intriguingly, however, the DNN model was not sufficient to explain scene categorization behavior, which was characterized by an additional strong contribution of functional information.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The findings highlight a limitation of current DNNs in explaining scene understanding.
source: This highlights a limitation of current DNNs in explaining scene understanding, as well as a potentially more distributed representation of scene information in the human brain beyond scene-selective cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the findings.

claim: There is a potentially more distributed representation of scene information in the human brain beyond scene-selective cortex.
source: This highlights a limitation of current DNNs in explaining scene understanding, as well as a potentially more distributed representation of scene information in the human brain beyond scene-selective cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the findings.

claim: Twenty healthy participants completed the first fMRI experiment and subsequent behavioral experiment.
source: Twenty healthy participants (13 female, mean age 25.4 years, SD = 4.6) completed the first fMRI experiment and subsequent behavioral experiment.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Eight participants completed the second fMRI experiment, four of whom also participated in Experiment 1.
source: Four of these participants (three female, mean age 24.3 years, SD = 4.6) additionally participated in the second fMRI experiment, as well as four new participants (two female, mean age 25 years, SD = 1.6), yielding a total of eight participants in this experiment.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Participants were scanned on a research-dedicated Siemens 7T Magnetom scanner.
source: Participants were scanned on a research-dedicated Siemens 7T Magnetom scanner in the Clinical Research Center on the National Institutes of Health Campus (Bethesda, MD).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Individual scenes were presented for a duration of 500 ms, separated by a 6 s interval.
source: Individual scenes were presented in an event-related design for a duration of 500 ms, separated by a 6 s interval.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants performed a task on the central fixation cross that was unrelated to the scenes.
source: In Experiment 1, participants performed a task on the central fixation cross that was unrelated to the scenes. Specifically, simultaneous with the presentation of each scene, either the vertical or horizontal arm of the fixation cross became slightly elongated and participants indicated which arm was longer by pressing one of two buttons indicated on a hand-held button box.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: In Experiment 2, participants were instructed to covertly name the scene whilst simultaneously pressing one button on the button box.
source: In Experiment 2, the fixation cross had a constant size, and participants were instructed to covertly name the scene whilst simultaneously pressing one button on the button box.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Participants completed eight experimental runs of 6.4 min each in both Experiment 1 and 2.
source: In both Experiment 1 and 2, participants completed eight experimental runs of 6.4 min each (192 TRs per run); one participant from Experiment 1 only completed seven runs due to time constraints.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Each run contained two exemplar presentations per scene category.
source: Each run contained two exemplar presentations per scene category.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: All stimuli were presented after two consecutive runs, yielding four presentations per exemplar in total.
source: Individual exemplars were balanced across runs such that all stimuli were presented after two consecutive runs, yielding four presentations per exemplar in total.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Participants additionally completed four independent functional block-design runs to localize scene-selective regions of interest.
source: Participants additionally completed four independent functional block-design runs (6.9 min, 208 TRs) that were used to localize scene-selective regions of interest (ROIs).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Scene-selective ROIs were generated by thresholding the statistical parametric maps resulting from contrasting scenes > faces at p<0.0001.
source: Scene-selective ROIs were generated by thresholding the statistical parametric maps resulting from contrasting scenes > faces at p<0.0001 (uncorrected).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: PPA and OPA were identified in all participants for both Experiment 1 and 2.
source: While PPA and OPA were identified in all participants for both Experiment 1 and 2, MPA/RSC was detected in only 14 out 20 participants in Experiment 1, and all analyses for this ROI in Experiment 1 are thus based on this subset of participants.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: MPA/RSC was detected in only 14 out 20 participants in Experiment 1.
source: While PPA and OPA were identified in all participants for both Experiment 1 and 2, MPA/RSC was detected in only 14 out 20 participants in Experiment 1, and all analyses for this ROI in Experiment 1 are thus based on this subset of participants.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) were computed based on pairwise cross-validated Mahalanobis distances between each of the 30 scene categories.
source: Specifically, we computed pairwise cross-validated Mahalanobis distances between each of the scene 30 categories following the approach outlined in (Walther et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citation support.

claim: Multi-variate noise normalization was applied by normalizing the beta-estimates by the covariance matrix of the residual time-courses between voxels within the ROI.
source: First, multi-variate noise normalization was applied by normalizing the beta-estimates by the covariance matrix of the residual time-courses between voxels within the ROI.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Cross-validated distances provide unbiased estimates of pattern dissimilarity on a ratio scale.
source: Note that unlike correlation distance measures, cross-validated distances provide unbiased estimates of pattern dissimilarity on a ratio scale (Walther et al., 2016), thus providing a distance measure suitable for direct model comparisons.
evidence: This is a methodological justification with citation support.

claim: The significance of correlations between model RDMs and fMRI RDMs was determined using one-sided signed-rank tests against zero.
source: To test the relatedness of the three models of scene dissimilarity with the measured fMRI dissimilarity, the off-diagonal elements of each model RDM were correlated (Pearson's r) with the off-diagonal elements of the RDMs of each individual participant's fMRI ROIs. Following (Nili et al., 2014), the significance of these correlations was determined using one-sided signed-rank tests against zero, while pairwise differences between models in terms of their correlation with fMRI dissimilarity were determined using two-sided signed-ranked tests.
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citation support.

claim: Pairwise differences between models were determined using two-sided signed-ranked tests.
source: Following (Nili et al., 2014), the significance of these correlations was determined using one-sided signed-rank tests against zero, while pairwise differences between models in terms of their correlation with fMRI dissimilarity were determined using two-sided signed-ranked tests.
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citation support.

claim: Noise ceilings were computed following Nili et al. (2014).
source: Noise ceilings were computed following (Nili et al., 2014): an upper bound was estimated by computing the correlation between each participant's individual RDM and the group-average RDM, while a lower bound was estimated by correlating each participant's RDM with the average RDM of the other participants (leave-one-out approach).
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citation support.

claim: Variance partitioning was performed by comparing the explained variance based on regression on individual models versus models in combination.
source: For the latter, the off-diagonal elements of each ROI RDM were assigned as the dependent variable, while the off-diagonal elements of the three model RDMs were entered as independent variables (predictors). To obtain unique and shared variance across the three models, seven multiple regression analyses were run in total: one 'full' regression that included all three feature models as predictors; and six reduced models that included as predictors either combinations of two models in pairs (e.g., functions and objects), or including each model by itself. By comparing the explained variance (r2) of a model used alone to the r2 of that model in conjunction with another model, we can infer the amount of variance that is independently explained by that model, that is partition the variance (see Groen et al., 2012; Ramakrishnan et al., 2014; Lescroart et al., 2015; Çukur et al., 2016; Greene et al., 2016; Hebart et al., 2018 for similar approaches).
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citation support.

claim: Whole-brain searchlight analyses were conducted to test the relatedness of functions, objects and visual feature models with fMRI activity recorded outside scene-selective ROIs.
source: To test the relatedness of functions, objects and visual feature models with fMRI activity recorded outside scene-selective ROIs, we conducted whole-brain searchlight analyses.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: RDMs were computed within spherical ROIs of 3 voxel diameter (i.e. 123 voxels/searchlight).
source: RDMs were computed in the same manner as for the ROI analysis, that is by computing cross-validated Mahalanobis distances based on multivariate noise-normalized multi-voxel patterns, but now within spherical ROIs of 3 voxel diameter (i.e. 123 voxels/searchlight).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Group-level significance was determined using Threshold Free Cluster Enhancement through Monte Carlo simulations.
source: Group-level significance was determined by submitting these surface maps to node-wise one-sample t-tests in conjunction with Threshold Free Cluster Enhancement (Smith and Nichols, 2009) through Monte Carlo simulations using the algorithm implemented in the CoSMoMVPA toolbox (Oosterhof et al., 2016), which performs group-level comparisons using sign-based permutation testing (n = 10,000) to correct for multiple comparisons.
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citation support.
